When physicists talk about The Theory of Everything and then ignore Music Theory, I think they're full of shit.
Actually, harmonic oscillation and the nice ratios that make up pitch intervals are pretty well covered by basic physics.
I'm not convinced that it is well covered.

Okay, let me break it down for you.

The human ear does a biological sort of Fourier transform to incoming sound, so we hear frequencies really well because of the way the masses and membranes in our ears move - but we hear phases of the component frequencies terribly. If you run a musical signal through an oscilloscope, you can see that the waveforms of different instruments are shaped differently, but run them through a fourier transform and you'll see that those shapes also have different harmonic and inharmonic overtones. If you generate a signal from those same tones at the correct amplitudes, but intentionally fuck up the phase shifts between them, it'll look different but sound indistinguishable.

So what really matters in human music theory is stimulating particular parts of the cochlea with the correct frequencies of vibrations. Well, what are the correct frequencies? Remember that the ear is sort of a mechanical FT filter, where different parts of the cochlea react to different frequencies (like how you can get the strings of a piano to vibrate by playing certain frequencies of sound near it). If we know what it does, we can predict how it will respond to given stimuli. The biggest thing is that a simple sound stimulates multiple areas of the cochlea, but quite specifically: The fundamental frequency, twice the fundamental frequency, three times the fundamental frequency, and so on.

Now consider the pitch intervals that make up nice, harmonic sounds. An octave: Hey, that's twice the frequency - the second harmonic! So an octave's harmonics line up with the base note's harmonics and the human ear hears "the same same stuff, but fuller" as certain less-scientifically-minded musicians and recording engineers say. How about a fifth? That's not a multiple of the base note, but it's a simple 3:2 ratio, so the third harmonic of the tonic and the second harmonic of the fifth are the same frequency, along with most of the other harmonics as you go up the frequencies. So what sounds good are notes that have nice, clean ratios between the notes because they fit the pattern of harmonics that's built into most tuned oscillators and the membranes that make up our ears.

Well, maybe you'd say to that "Well, there's a ratio between any two numbers, so that doesn't make any predictions about what would sound bad." Okay, I'll go the other way: Simple sounds light up a whole series of sensitive cells in our ears, so if good intervals are intervals that make the two series of frequencies match up, maybe bad intervals are intervals that make the series of frequencies mismatch as much as possible. So go searching for two such frequencies. Now, I'll admit there's one caveat here: The theoretically-worst match would be two frequencies that are almost the same, but infinitesimally different. Technically, these would be extraordinarily bad matches because none of the frequencies would be exactly the same. But that prediction is based on purely mathematical prediction without regard for the physical reality of sound waves and oscillating structures. The sensitive parts of our ears are physical oscillators that are excited by waves coming in, and physical oscillators are energized by frequencies very close to their "actual" frequency, as well as that frequency itself. So what actually sounds the worst is not a sound with all the harmonics infinitesimally different from the harmonics of the tonic, but a sound where the harmonics are just different enough that our ears pick up the differences. If you limit yourself to frequencies that are on a chromatic scale, this is the tritone. If not, it's just the same note played on a badly-tuned instrument. Hey, it works!

So that's all biology, what about the physics? Well, I have two answers to that.

First answer: All of these frequencies and harmonic series and stuff springs out of the physics of simple oscillators. At its simplest, an oscillator in physics is a mass and a force that pushes the mass back to its resting position in proportion to its displacement from that position. With these two things, you have a simple harmonic oscillator that puts out a particular frequency of vibration. But, again, even simple instruments are not that simple. Two big things change the way the system behaves: If the forces acting on the mass are non-linear, and if the "mass" is not actually a single mass on a spring, but a lot of masses connected together by springs. And hey, would you look at that? If you introduce nonlinearities into the oscillator, what do you get? You get an oscillator that doesn't put out a simple sine wave that has a single frequency anymore: The oscillator makes a different waveform, perhaps squishing the crests and troughs of said sine wave. Run that through a fourier transform and oh my god would you look at that? It's that same series of frequencies you get in the harmonics of a musical note. Because that's what those frequencies are: The frequencies that you have to add up to make a waveform of an arbitrary shape. Next, consider what happens when you connect multiple masses together with springs: The masses will move together, and for some configurations, the motions of the masses will reinforce each other and move smoothly, while others will end up with some of the masses moving against the others and damping out the vibrations of the oscillator overall. Oh, hey, this describes the design of musical instruments pretty well: The arrangements of masses and springs that resonate well and move in harmony happen to be things like a string stretched on a frame, or a bar of metal vibrating in free space. Actually, go one step further: It turns out that these little masses are atoms, if you zoom in enough! Every atom in a lump of metal is acted upon by the atoms around it by electromagnetic forces that make it move almost exactly like a lead weight hanging from springs, so it turns out the forces that govern the motion of atoms actually do explain the behavior of oscillators made up of atoms, such as musical instruments and the human ear.

Second answer: Not only are the instruments and your ears made up of atoms that the "theory of everything" would explain, so is your brain, your mp3 player, and every goddamn other thing in the universe. If that's not good enough for you and you're going to complain that the "theory of everything" doesn't explain why you prefer bananas or strawberries right along with why some sounds are nicer than others, you're being willfully obtuse and you can go eat an entire bag of dicks.
